adds.title: N.S. transgender prisoner looking to challenge decision to hold her in men's prison - Saltwire / The Chronicle Herald
adds.summary: The Chronicle Herald reports (18 March 2025) that a federal judge gave a transgender woman from the Halifax region more time to file her application for judicial review of the decision to hold her in a men's prison while she serves a two-year robbery sentence; the judge cited a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted the applicant's access to her lawyer. This is the documented Nova Scotia case showing how a trans woman's correctional placement is being challenged and judicially reviewed in the province's custodial system.

adds.title: Grants to Support 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Groups, Provincial Conference - Government of Nova Scotia
adds.summary: The Government of Nova Scotia announced (10 June 2026) more than $176,000 through the first round of its new 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, with awards including $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth and $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, plus $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference; per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year. This is official, dated evidence of provincial funding and institutional support for 2SLGBTQIA+ communities across Nova Scotia.

adds.title: Province Releases First 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan - Government of Nova Scotia
adds.summary: The Government of Nova Scotia released (8 January 2026) the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022 - described as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people - and informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations; the plan maps actions to improve programs and policies and support full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people. This is official confirmation that Nova Scotia operates an explicit provincial inclusion framework rather than restrictive trans-specific legislation.

adds.title: Quebec's new trans inmate policy goes against human rights, advocates say - CBC News
adds.summary: CBC News reports (19 June 2025) that Quebec's public security minister announced transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities, in a directive issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison; advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This is dated, province-specific evidence of an official Quebec policy change reversing the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

adds.title: Gender Identity Protected by the Quebec Charter of Rights - Éducaloi
adds.summary: Éducaloi reports that on 10 June 2024 Quebec's Human Rights Tribunal found a Montreal bar discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training; the page notes gender identity and expression were added as prohibited grounds of discrimination under Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms in 2016, and cites 2021 census data that 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older (0.27% of those aged 15-34) identify as transgender. This is Quebec-specific enforcement evidence that trans people can win discrimination claims under provincial law.

adds.title: Center for Gender Advocacy and al. v. Attorney General of Quebec - IMK
adds.summary: IMK's case note on Centre for Gender Advocacy and al. v. Attorney General of Quebec records that after a two-month trial with 29 witnesses the Quebec Superior Court (2021 QCCS 191) declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people, that the Court of Appeal largely upheld the decision (2024 QCCA 348), and that the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code. It is a dated, lawyer-verified account of the landmark Quebec court outcome that reshaped the province's rules on sex designation and identity documents.

adds.title: 'Parents must be fully involved' in student's decision to change pronouns, Ontario education minister says - CTV News
adds.summary: CTV News reports (28 August 2023) that Ontario's education minister, Stephen Lecce, said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronouns at school, speaking the same week Saskatchewan joined New Brunswick in legislating parental consent for students under 16 who want to change names and pronouns; Lecce added that teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child, and Ontario did not adopt such legislation at that time. The article documents the Ontario government's stance on pronoun and name rules in schools at the peak of the 2023 Canadian pronoun-policy wave - the province held the line against legislating parental consent.

adds.title: Policy on preventing discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression - Ontario Human Rights Commission
adds.summary: The Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the Ontario Human Rights Code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations; it defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender, and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. The policy is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.
